name: Marshallese
notes: Marshallese (Kajin Ṃajeḷ), a Micronesian language of the Marshall Islands. ORTHOGRAPHY: the map reads the 'new' standard orthography of the Marshallese-English Dictionary (Abo, Bender, Capelle & DeBrum 1976) in both of its letterform families — the Marshallese-English Online Dictionary writes ⟨ḷ ṃ ṇ ñ ọ⟩ with dots below, the print standard writes the same letters with cedillas and a macron, ⟨ļ m̧ ņ n̄ o̧⟩, and both spellings are keyed. CONSONANTS: every consonant carries a secondary articulation. ⟨p b⟩ = /pʲ pˠ/, ⟨j t⟩ = /tʲ tˠ/, ⟨m ṃ⟩ = /mʲ mˠ/, ⟨n ṇ⟩ = /nʲ nˠ/, ⟨l ḷ⟩ = /lʲ lˠ/, ⟨d r⟩ = /rʲ rˠ/, ⟨ñ⟩ = /ŋ/. A following ⟨w⟩ marks the rounded series (⟨kw ñw ṇw ḷw rw⟩ = /kʷ ŋʷ nʷ lʷ rʷ/) and after ⟨b ṃ⟩ merely restates the velarisation of the bilabial, so ⟨w⟩ is an independent /w/ only word-initially or between vowels. VOWELS: the language has four vowel phonemes /i e ɛ æ/ that contrast in height alone and are unspecified for backness and rounding; their front, back-unrounded and rounded surface qualities are supplied by the flanking consonants' secondary articulation (Bender 1968, 1969; Choi 1992; Willson 2003). The spelling records the surface quality rather than the phoneme, so the nine vowel letters are a height row crossed with a backness column, and the column names the articulation of whatever stands beside the vowel: ⟨i e ā⟩ are palatalised-flanked, ⟨ū ō a⟩ velarised-flanked, ⟨u o ọ⟩ rounded-flanked. The height rows are ⟨i ū u⟩ = /i/ and ⟨ā a ọ⟩ = /æ/; the middle row ⟨e ō o⟩ spells /ɛ/ and /e/ alike, an under-differentiation the spelling cannot resolve, so those letters are list-valued with /ɛ/ first — /ɛ/ is the more frequent reading of each of the three letters in the WikiPron Marshallese gold (⟨e⟩ 181 of 326, ⟨ō⟩ 123 of 181, ⟨o⟩ 139 of 309). The surface qualities live in `allophones`, where they belong: /i/ → [i ɯ u], /e/ → [e ə o], /ɛ/ → [ɛ ʌ ɔ], /æ/ → [æ ɑ ɒ]. GLIDES: no Marshallese syllable begins or ends with a bare vowel. Where the flanking articulation has no consonant to sit on — at a word edge, or between two written vowels — the matching glide /j ɰ w/ is the segment that carries it, and the spelling leaves it unwritten because /ɰ/ never surfaces phonetically and /j w/ do so only erratically. The positional entries state this: a vowel letter takes its column's glide before it word-initially, after it word-finally, and — for ⟨a⟩, the letter a written ⟨ia⟩/⟨ua⟩ hiatus actually joins — the PRECEDING vowel's column glide when one is written before it (⟨iaļ⟩ 'road' is /jijælˠ/: ⟨i⟩'s own /j/ carries over, it does not restate ⟨a⟩'s own velarised /ɰ/). This one grapheme's split is as far as the positional vocabulary reaches: ``after_front_vowel``/``after_back_vowel`` classify the PRECEDING vowel letter by stripping it to its bare Latin base, and that stripping conflates ⟨a⟩ with ⟨ā⟩ (opposite columns sharing one base letter) and the rounded column ⟨u o ọ⟩ with the velarised one (both bases classified 'back'); declaring the split on every vowel grapheme measurably regresses more words than it fixes (see RESIDUE), so only ⟨a⟩ carries it, and every other vowel letter still takes its OWN column's glide after a vowel, exactly as before. The WikiPron Marshallese gold agrees closely with word-initial and word-final position: 215 of 217 word-initial and 291 of 292 word-final vowel letters carry exactly the glide their column predicts. A doubled vowel letter is therefore V-glide-V, not a long vowel: ⟨naaj⟩ 'future' is /nʲæɰætʲ/. RESIDUE: several things the spelling genuinely does not determine, or that the positional vocabulary cannot express. Between vowel letters of DIFFERENT columns other than ⟨a⟩ the sequence may carry one glide or two (⟨ai⟩ is /…ɰj…/ 34 times and a single glide 14 times in the gold), and only one is written; the map emits the following vowel's glide there, per the paragraph above. A vowel letter that is BOTH word-final and the second half of a written hiatus loses its internal glide entirely: ``word_final`` and ``after_vowel`` are declared on the same grapheme and only the higher-ranked ``word_final`` fires, so ⟨ae⟩ 'to swim' comes out /ɰæɛj/ where the gold has /ɰæjɛj/ — the positional vocabulary has no combined 'word-final AND after-vowel' condition to declare instead. This class covers roughly 60 of the 947 WikiPron gold words, none scored exactly. A related, currently unimplemented gap: a rounded vowel immediately before a consonant that starts the next syllable can leave its own /w/ off-glide unwritten before that consonant (⟨Ļora⟩ is /lˠɛwrˠæɰ/, not the /lˠɛrˠæɰ/ the map currently gives), which is a pre-consonantal glide the map has no position for at all, distinct from the vowel-vowel hiatus cases above. And a consonant with no letter of its own for the rounded series — ⟨k ñ⟩, and ⟨r ḷ ṇ⟩ when no ⟨w⟩ follows — is rounded when every vowel letter beside it is in the rounded column, which the positional vocabulary cannot express as a single condition; the map leaves those plain (⟨k⟩ is /kʷ/ in 50 of the 68 such gold tokens). Stops are partially voiced between vowels when not geminated ([b d ɡ]) and ⟨j⟩ is usually a voiced fricative [zʲ] word-internally, both recorded in `allophones`. INPUT CONTRACT: text in the new orthography, either letterform family. Old-orthography text (⟨dr⟩, ⟨b⟩ for both /pʲ pˠ/, no diacritics) is out of scope and must be converted upstream.
